chapter: Chicago in the 1950s: Mercury, unions and jobbing
title: The Mercury date, Grandpa's Spells and Liberace
summary: Hodes records for Mercury through an agent. After Liberace recorded Grandpa's Spells first, his record came out later.

bands.name: Art Hodes and His High Fivers

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: So I have to go get a small band because they will pay for a small band, and maybe get a vocal in there and some sort of entertainment. And this is what I'm doing continuously. And with ups and downs. And meanwhile, I get a date from Mercury, the Hot Fivers, they gave me that date. And that's through an agent, again. He was able to maneuver a date. And this is -- it gives you a little picture of what the music business is like.

One of the tunes I decided to record, of course, is 'Grandpa Spells.' And I think the A&R man was David something, I'm not sure. But he was also a pianist, had his own band. Anyway, I recorded this record and 'Sweet Georgia Brown' and other things. And for those times -- and it still is a good
record, for what it started out to be. It's concise, it's more like a John Kirby band.
Is that Art Hodes and his High Fivers?

And for what it started out to do, it was tight and crisp, and I wouldn't call it traditional jazz and the purists probably didn't like it. But there was a lot of people that liked it and bought it. And the record don't come out. We wait month after month after month and it's still ain't out.

Now I go up to Minneapolis to play a date, and somebody says, hey, you play 'Grandpa's Spells', I just heard it by Liberace. And then I get back to Chicago and the band leader, the A&R man, has put out a record. What they did was, they heard me do 'Grandpa's Spells', and they loved the material. So somebody got Liberace to do it. Then their A&R man did it, then after they milked it, then they put out my record.
